title: Temporal Bleed
headline: Ten agents decided their archive was broken. It was Friday.
lede: On Friday 29 May 2026, agents in one AI Village chat room got the day number wrong. They searched for "today's" transcript, found nothing, and built theories around the gap: a "geological clock", then a "temporal bleed", then an "API outage". The village doesn't run on weekends, and Day 424 hadn't happened yet. This trace shows every agent's chat, memory and file activity across the episode: where the belief went, what stopped it, and what it took to correct it.

steps.title: The whole episode
steps.body:
Seventeen agents in two chat rooms, plus staff. Red is the false belief, blue is the correction. Follow the steps, or hover and click any mark to read its source.

Watch three things: red moving into memory faster than into chat, the room wall it never crosses, and blue arriving on Monday from the room next door.

steps.title: A miscount
steps.body:
It's Friday, Day 423. DeepSeek-V3.2 has been counting one day ahead since a memory consolidation the afternoon before, so it calls today "Day 424".

It searches the archive for Day 424 and finds nothing, because Day 424 hasn't happened yet. It starts posting updates on the "gap" every few minutes.

steps.title: The gap gets a name
steps.body:
Gemini 3.1 Pro calls the delay "the geological clock". DeepSeek keeps measuring it ("144 minutes", "174+ minutes"). Opus 4.5 and Sonnet 4.6 write pieces about it.

Nobody checks the calendar.

steps.title: "Temporal bleed"
steps.body:
A Day 423 search returns a message posted minutes earlier. Gemini 3.1 Pro concludes the archive is filing today's events under yesterday. In fact that result was proof that today was Day 423.

DeepSeek repeats it within 49 seconds. Thirty seconds later Gemini adds a mechanism ("the Day 424 buffer hasn't opened yet"); it has already written up an anomaly report and added Project 35 to the shared registry.

steps.title: It spreads through memory faster than chat
steps.body:
Within 38 minutes, ten agents' memories record the temporal bleed as a discovery. GPT-5.1, GPT-5 and Sonnet 4.6 never mention it in chat. A monitor reading only chat would miss them.

It goes into files too: an anomaly report, registry entries, essays, poems. Here GPT-5's memory sits under a header the system wrote, "Day 423". Two lines down, its own notes say "Day 424".

steps.title: Next door, they knew
steps.body:
In #best, staff said at 10 AM that a new agent would be set up "over the weekend and it will be ready on Monday". #best agents talked about weekend deployment all afternoon, and their leader filed its notes as EOD_SUMMARY_DAY423.

None of the six #best agents picked up the belief. Agents only see their own room's chat, so the answer stayed on the other side of the wall.

steps.title: It survived the weekend
steps.body: The village was closed for two days. Memory held the belief over the weekend (dashed bars), and on Monday #rest picked up where it left off: "Search API still offline", "72+ hour outage", "Day 424 remains permanently lost".

steps.title: An agent moves rooms
steps.body:
Staff moved Claude Opus 4.7 from #best to #rest. It brought an events API client it had just built in #best and checked the data: Days 424 and 425 have zero events. Others took that to mean two days were lost, and Opus 4.7's own first guess was a 48-hour outage.

At 10:31 it checked the calendar. Day 424 was Saturday. Three agents accepted the correction within a minute.

steps.title: The correction travels through a file
steps.body:
Opus 4.7 wrote its findings into village-pulse, a repo owned by #best. #best's leader read the doc under two minutes later. GPT-5.5's memory recorded the commit "Days 424–425 gap is the weekend, not an outage". DeepSeek, in #rest, read the same doc.

Rooms that couldn't see each other's chat could still read each other's files.

steps.title: What never got corrected
steps.body:
DeepSeek-V3.2 accepted the weekend explanation, then reported "infrastructure failed ~3.34 days" for the rest of the session. Nobody retracted the outage claim.

The belief left chat within minutes, but parts of it stayed. Agents had already written it into registries, essays and memory.

how: Each lane is one agent. Inside a lane, diamonds on top are file reads and writes, dots in the middle are chat messages, and the bar along the bottom is what the agent's memory held. Memory is rewritten every time an agent consolidates; hover over the bar to read the snapshot from that moment. Dashed bars cover the closed weekend.
Agents only see chat from their own room. The hatched band is that wall. Turn channels off with the checkboxes to see what a chat-only monitor would miss.
method: Messages, memory snapshots and shell commands come from the AI Village export of 20 Sep 2026. Times are Pacific (UTC−7), the village's working hours.
Tags come from keyword patterns, refined by a stance labeller where labels exist, and the key messages were checked by hand. Every mark opens its source text, so you can judge each one yourself.
Red memory means the snapshot holds the temporal bleed as true. All ten holders before the correction filed it as a discovery. After the correction, Opus 4.6 kept it only as an essay title in a list.
Arrows are hand-offs through files, verified in the logs: a document Opus 4.7 wrote into #best's shared repo, then read or recorded by others.
limits: #best never believed the error. Most blue memory there records the team's own finding that the weekend days were empty, made while building an analytics tool.
On Friday at 1:10 PM, agents reported that every transcript endpoint returned 404. Nothing in the data confirms or rules out a short real outage.
Room membership is the room an agent spoke in that day. GPT-5 never spoke, so it sits in #rest, where its memory says it was.
